candidates.title: Part of the disconnect is that the name “data” massively undersells what it truly represents in model development. People who are not close to model development think of data as this inert commodity you buy and shovel into a model, like coal. In reality great data encodes incredibly high value knowledge, taste and expertise, often articulated and structured in ways that did not exist previously. This makes it one of THE fundamental building blocks for creating increasingly capable intelligence across domains. Data will continue to be incredibly central to the intelligence industry .

candidates.title: This is a pretty key insight. Services businesses are always held back by their ability to deliver outcomes to customers. That scaling essentially only could come from headcount, and no matter how much demand you saw, there was always a finite amount of talent you could get for the problem you were going after. Not to mention, the customer generally always wants the work done faster, at a lower price, or at a higher quality. Agents entirely change the calculus here, because now we can scale output in a way that’s decoupled from the among of time that goes in. A single engineer can have the output of dozens of engineers before. A single designer can probably build out your entire design system and brand. And so on. Well why isn’t this just all agents then? Because the key is to still have experts on the front end that actually can ensure the right outcomes are delivered from agents. It’s likely that we’re going to see this in a wide variety of categories. You’ll see this in cyber security, advertising and marketing, legal, accounting, IT transformation, and a number of other historically people-only services industries. It’s a great time if you’re starting one of these businesses, or if you have the capability to transform an existing one.

candidates.title: New research from Replit on scaling laws for agent swarms. We show that scaling the number of agents can yield dramatic performance gains, but unlike traditional scaling laws, more compute doesn't necessarily translate into better results, and how agents organize themselves matters. - Given a fixed two-hour window, Opus 5.5 went from a 3.7x speedup on NumPy with one agent to 18.9x with 32 agents. - GPT-6.2 Astra was the strongest solo agent but exhibited negative scaling beyond 8 agents. - Models spontaneously developed different organizational structures. Decentralized swarms scaled better than those that relied on centralized coordination. - The parallelizability of the problem was a strong predictor of swarm performance. - Interestingly, individual model intelligence is a poor predictor of collective intelligence. We’re also open-sourcing Optimization-Bench to advance research into this new dimension of inference-time scaling. https://t.co/RXBU7aM5FE
